case_prompt: An 84‐year‐old man presented with acute onset abdominal and back pain that began during the night without vomiting or gastrointestinal disturbance. One day earlier he had completed a 10-day course of clindamycin for left calf cellulitis. His medical history included atrial fibrillation, congestive cardiac failure, ulcerative colitis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent deep vein thromboses; he was on maintenance warfarin. On examination he was afebrile, blood pressure 200/132 mm Hg, heart rate 68 beats/min, and capillary blood glucose 9.1 mmol/L. Chest auscultation was clear; abdominal examination showed mild to moderate epigastric tenderness with normal bowel sounds; mild resolving cellulitis of the right calf was noted. Admission studies revealed hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 12.9×10^9/L, platelets 303×10^9/L, INR 6.8, urea 8.7 mmol/L, creatinine 111 μmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, CRP 75 mg/L, calcium 2.02 mmol/L. ECG showed a paced rhythm and chest radiograph demonstrated slight fluid overload, cardiomegaly, and interstitial shadowing. The initial impression was possible gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Warfarin was withheld, vitamin K administered, and intravenous fluids started. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed subtle, non-specific bilateral adrenal enhancing lesions. His INR normalized to 2–3, but he remained hypotensive with ongoing abdominal pain, nausea, lethargy, and abdominal distension; capillary blood glucose remained normal despite withholding diabetic medications. A short synacthen test showed no appreciable rise in cortisol (baseline 95 nmol/L; 60 min 113 nmol/L; 90 min 132 nmol/L).

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease was initially considered because of epigastric pain — “The initial impression was possible gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.” 2. Sepsis was considered given elevated inflammatory markers and co-morbidities — “…it was important to rule out sepsis or malignancy.” 3. Malignancy was considered due to age, presentation, and risk factors — “…it was important to rule out sepsis or malignancy.” 4. Adrenal metastases were considered based on CT findings of bilateral adrenal lesions — “the differential diagnosis for which included metastases, infection, granulomatous disease or haemorrhage.” 5. selection.screen_reason: Abdominal and back pain with hypotension, supratherapeutic INR on warfarin for antiphospholipid syndrome, bilateral adrenal lesions and a failed synacthen test give bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
selection.second_look_note: Acute abdominal and back pain on warfarin for antiphospholipid syndrome with a supratherapeutic INR directs CT and a short synacthen test, which show bilateral adrenal lesions and adrenal failure.
